title: Using Sex Toys: Is It Allowed in the Bible?
paragraphs:
Using Sex Toys: Is It Allowed in the Bible?
The Question Many Christians Are Afraid to Ask—And the Answer Might Challenge More Than Your Actions
There are questions many believers will ask publicly.
Questions about prayer.
Questions about church.
Questions about faith.
Then there are the questions whispered into search bars at midnight.
Questions people feel embarrassed to ask their pastor.
Questions married couples discuss behind closed doors.
Questions single believers wrestle with in silence.
Questions that carry shame before they even receive an answer.
One of those questions is this:
"Are sex toys allowed in the Bible?"
The reason this question matters is not because Christians are obsessed with rules.
It matters because followers of Jesus genuinely want to honor God with every area of life—including sexuality.
And before we rush to an answer, we must first acknowledge something important.
The Bible never specifically mentions modern sex toys.
Not once.
There is no verse that says, "You shall not use a vibrator."
There is no verse that says, "You may use this device in marriage."
So if we are going to answer honestly, we cannot invent commands God never gave.
At the same time, we cannot ignore biblical principles simply because technology has changed.
The question is not merely:
"Does the Bible mention sex toys?"
The deeper question is:
"Does this glorify Christ?"
That changes everything.
The Bible consistently presents sexuality as God's creation, not Satan's invention.
In Genesis 1:27, God created humanity as male and female.
In Genesis 2:24 we read:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew phrase is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad).
It literally means "one flesh."
This is not merely physical union.
It describes covenant intimacy.
A complete joining.
A God-designed bond.
Sex was never intended to be merely an act of pleasure.
Pleasure is part of God's gift.
But the ultimate purpose is covenantal unity, love, self-giving, and reflection of God's design.
That foundation is critical because every sexual question must begin there.
Not with desire.
Not with culture.
Not with personal preference.
With God's purpose.
When we move into the New Testament, the apostle Paul writes:
The Greek phrase for "glory" is δόξα (doxa).
It refers to honor, splendor, reputation, and praise.
The Christian's central question is not:
"What can I get away with?"
The Christian's question is:
"Does this bring honor to Jesus Christ?"
That principle alone immediately eliminates many sexual practices because they are rooted in lust, selfishness, pornography, fantasy, adultery of the heart, or idolatry.
Jesus Himself said:
"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." (Matthew 5:28)
The Greek word translated "lust" is ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō).
It means a craving, coveting, or consuming desire.
The issue is not attraction.
The issue is sinful desire that seeks self-gratification apart from God's design.
This becomes an important measuring rod when discussing sex toys.

If a person is using sex toys while consuming pornography, fantasizing about someone who is not their spouse, engaging in sexual sin outside marriage, or feeding addictive behaviors, Scripture clearly condemns those actions.
The problem is not merely the object.
The problem is the heart.
Jesus consistently went deeper than behavior.
He addressed motives.
Intentions.
Desires.
Hidden idols.
This is where many discussions become uncomfortable.
Because Christians often want a list.
God frequently gives principles.
Consider married couples.
The Bible teaches that husband and wife belong to one another sexually.
Paul writes:
A few verses later he explains that neither spouse has exclusive authority over their own body but serves the other in love.
The biblical picture is mutual affection, mutual sacrifice, and mutual care.
Within that covenant relationship, Scripture gives remarkable freedom while maintaining holiness.
The Bible celebrates marital intimacy in the Song of Songs with language so passionate that many modern Christians blush when reading it.
God is not embarrassed by marital intimacy.
He invented it.
The question then becomes whether a particular practice strengthens covenant intimacy or replaces it.
Does it increase loving connection?
Or does it encourage isolation?
Does it promote selflessness?
Or selfishness?
Does it deepen marital unity?
Or create dependency on something outside the relationship?
Different Christian believers and theologians have reached different conclusions here.

Some conclude that certain sex toys used mutually within marriage can be morally permissible if they serve the marital relationship, do not involve pornography, do not replace one's spouse, and do not become an idol.
Others conclude they should be avoided entirely because they believe they shift intimacy away from God's intended design.
Both positions attempt to apply biblical principles.
The Bible itself does not explicitly settle the question.
Therefore believers should exercise humility and avoid speaking where Scripture is silent with greater certainty than Scripture itself.
At the same time, Scripture does provide warnings about the human heart.
Anything can become an idol.
Money.
Food.
Entertainment.
Ministry.
Even good gifts.
An idol is anything that begins to take the place God should occupy.
The apostle John closes his first epistle with a striking command:
"Little children, keep yourselves from idols." (1 John 5:21)
Notice he does not provide a list.
Because idols constantly change forms.
The human heart is an idol factory.
A believer must honestly ask:
"Would I be content if this disappeared tomorrow?"
"Has this become necessary for my satisfaction?"
"Is my dependence growing on Christ or on something else?"
Those questions matter.
Because holiness is not merely about avoiding bad things.
It is about loving Jesus above all things.
For single Christians, the conversation becomes even more serious.
The Bible consistently reserves sexual expression for marriage.
Paul writes:
The Greek word is πορνεία (porneia).
It encompasses sexual activity outside God's design for marriage.
Modern culture often treats sexual fulfillment as a necessity.
Scripture treats holiness as a priority.
That does not mean the struggle is easy.
It means obedience remains possible through the power of Christ.
Many believers carry private battles.
Temptations.
Loneliness.
Desires.
Shame.
Yet the Gospel does not merely command purity.
The Gospel provides power for purity.
The heart of Christianity is not behavior modification.
It is transformation.
That is why this discussion cannot end with sex toys.
It must end with Jesus.
Because every sexual question eventually becomes a worship question.
Who sits on the throne of your heart?
What are you seeking most?
Comfort?
Pleasure?
Escape?
Validation?
Relief?
Or Christ?
The Bible's ultimate message is not that sinners must clean themselves up before coming to God.
The Bible's message is that sinners run to Christ because they cannot save themselves.
That is the story of Scripture.
Abraham failed.
David fell.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet Jesus rewrote their stories.
That is why our ministry theme matters so deeply.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps while reading this article you expected a simple yes-or-no answer.
Instead, Scripture asks a more penetrating question.
Not merely:
"What are you doing?"
But:
"Who are you becoming?"
The goal of the Christian life is not to stand as close to sin as possible without crossing a line.
The goal is to become more like Jesus.
That pursuit changes every decision.
Every relationship.
Every desire.
Every private moment.
And every question we bring before God.
If this article challenged you, encouraged you, or helped you think biblically about a difficult topic, do not keep it to yourself.
You are helping spread the Gospel, strengthen believers, equip disciples, and point people toward Jesus Christ in a world desperate for truth.
And do not leave without sharing your voice.
"Christ is still shaping me"
if you desire to honor God even in the areas of life that are difficult to discuss.
Your testimony may encourage someone else who feels alone in their struggle.
Because sometimes freedom begins when someone finally realizes they are not the only one fighting.
The questions you hide from everyone else are often the very places where Jesus wants to meet you.
